column2: On the authority of Abū Najīḥ al-ʿIrbāḍ ibn Sāriyah (may Allah be pleased with him), who said: The Messenger of Allah ﷺ gave us a deeply moving admonition at which our hearts trembled and our eyes shed tears. We said: “O Messenger of Allah,

it is as though this were a farewell admonition, so advise us.” He said: “I advise you to fear Allah, the Mighty and Majestic, and to hear and obey, even if a slave is put in command over you. For whoever of you lives will see much disagreement. So hold to my Sunnah and the Sunnah of the rightly guided, guiding caliphs; bite onto it with your molar teeth. And beware of newly invented matters,
for every innovation is misguidance.” Reported by Abū Dāwūd and al-Tirmidhī, who said: “A ḥasan ṣaḥīḥ hadith.”

Al-ʿIrbāḍ's words, “The Messenger of Allah ﷺ gave us a deeply moving admonition at which our hearts trembled and our eyes shed tears”: an admonition is speech containing encouragement and warning which affects the soul and reaches the heart, so that it trembles in fear of Allah.

Al-ʿIrbāḍ (may Allah be pleased with him) described this admonition with these three qualities: eloquence, the trembling of the heart and the shedding of tears. Ibn Rajab said in Jāmiʿ al-ʿUlūm wa-l-Ḥikam (2/111): “Eloquence in admonition is commendable,

because it is closer to being accepted by the heart and winning it. Eloquence is succeeding in conveying the intended meanings and bringing them to the hearts of the listeners in the best form of words that express them, the most articulate, the sweetest to the ear and the most affecting to the heart.”
Allah described the believers as having trembling hearts and tearful eyes at the mention of Allah. Allah, the Mighty and Majestic, said:

“The believers are only those who, when Allah is mentioned, their hearts tremble, and when His verses are recited to them, it increases them in faith, and upon their Lord they rely” [al-Anfāl 8:2]; and He said: “And when they hear what has been sent down to the Messenger, you see their eyes overflowing with tears” [al-Māʾidah 5:83].
His words, “We said: O Messenger of Allah,

it is as though this were a farewell admonition, so advise us”: that is, this exhortation resembled the admonition of one bidding farewell. So the noble Companions, eager as they were for every good, asked for a comprehensive piece of advice that the Messenger of Allah ﷺ would entrust to them, which they could hold fast to and rely on,
because advice given at parting has a special effect on the soul. Perhaps this admonition contained something that suggested a farewell, which is why they asked for this advice.

His words, “I advise you to fear Allah”: fear of Allah, the Mighty and Majestic, is for a person to place between himself and the anger of Allah a shield that protects him from it, by doing acts of obedience, avoiding acts of disobedience

and believing the reports [of revelation]. It is Allah's counsel to the first and the last, as Allah, the Mighty and Majestic, said: “And We have already counselled those who were given the Book before you, and you, to fear Allah” [al-Nisāʾ 4:131].

It is the cause of all good and success in this world and the Hereafter. The command to fear Allah comes in many verses, especially those beginning “O you who believe”, and likewise in the advice of the Messenger of Allah ﷺ to his Companions.
His words, “and to hear and obey, even if a slave is put in command over you”: this is advice to hear and obey those in authority, except in disobedience to Allah, even if the commander is a slave.

The scholars are unanimous that a slave is not eligible for the caliphate. This hadith, and others with the same meaning, are understood as stressing in the strongest terms the duty to hear and obey a slave if he were caliph,
even though that does not happen; or as referring to a caliph appointing a slave over a town or a group; or as meaning that he was free when he was appointed
and is called a slave because of what he had been; or as referring to a slave who has seized power over people by force, after which affairs have settled and security has been established,
because contending with him would bring about what is worse than his rule.
His words, “For whoever of you lives will see much disagreement”: this is one of the proofs of his prophethood ﷺ, for he foretold something in the future that happened exactly as he ﷺ said;

those Companions of the Prophet ﷺ who lived long saw much disagreement and departure from what the Messenger of Allah ﷺ and his Companions were upon, with the appearance of some misguided sects, such as the Qadariyyah, the Khawārij and others.
His words, “So hold to my Sunnah and the Sunnah of the rightly guided, guiding caliphs; bite onto it with your molar teeth”: having foretold that division would come about and become widespread,

he ﷺ pointed to the way of safety and salvation, which is holding fast to his Sunnah and the Sunnah of his rightly guided caliphs. His rightly guided caliphs are Abū Bakr, ʿUmar, ʿUthmān and ʿAlī (may Allah be pleased with them).

The Messenger of Allah ﷺ described their caliphate as a caliphate of prophethood, as in the hadith of Safīnah (may Allah be pleased with him): “The caliphate of prophethood will be thirty years; then Allah will give kingship—or His kingship—to whom He wills.” Reported by Abū Dāwūd (4646) and others.

It is an authentic hadith; al-Albānī included it in al-Silsilah al-Ṣaḥīḥah (460) and quoted nine scholars who declared it authentic. Ibn Rajab said (2/120): “The Sunnah is the path followed, so this includes holding fast to the beliefs, deeds and words that he and his rightly guided caliphs were upon.

This is the complete Sunnah. That is why the Salaf of old applied the name Sunnah only to what includes all of that; this meaning is reported from al-Ḥasan, al-Awzāʿī and al-Fuḍayl ibn ʿIyāḍ. Many later scholars restrict the name Sunnah to what relates to beliefs,
because they are the foundation of the religion, and whoever opposes them is in great danger.”
The Messenger of Allah ﷺ urged holding fast to his Sunnah and the Sunnah of his rightly guided caliphs with his word “hold to” (ʿalaykum), a verbal noun with the force of a command;
then he indicated how firmly to hold it with his words, “bite onto it with your molar teeth”. Al-nawājidh are the molars, and this is an emphatic way of expressing how firmly to hold fast to it.
His words, “And beware of newly invented matters,
for every innovation is misguidance”: in the narration of Abū Dāwūd (4607): “And beware of newly invented matters,

for every newly invented matter is an innovation, and every innovation is misguidance.” Newly invented matters are things invented and innovated in the religion that have no basis in it. This goes back to the blameworthy disagreement and division the Prophet ﷺ mentioned in his words,
“For whoever of you lives will see much disagreement.” The Prophet ﷺ described all innovations as misguidance, so no innovation is good,

because of the generality of his words, “and every innovation is misguidance”. Muḥammad ibn Naṣr reported in his book al-Sunnah, with an authentic chain, that Ibn ʿUmar (may Allah be pleased with them both) said: “Every innovation is misguidance,

even if people see it as good.” Al-Shāṭibī mentioned in al-Iʿtiṣām from Ibn al-Mājishūn, who said: I heard Mālik say: “Whoever introduces into Islam an innovation that he considers good has claimed that Muḥammad betrayed the message,
because Allah says: ‘This day I have perfected for you your religion’ [al-Māʾidah 5:3]. So whatever was not religion on that day is not religion today.” Abū ʿUthmān al-Naysābūrī said:
“Whoever makes the Sunnah his master in word and deed speaks with wisdom, and whoever makes whim his master in word and deed speaks with innovation”

(see Ḥilyat al-Awliyāʾ, 10/244). As for the hadith reported by Muslim in his Ṣaḥīḥ (1017), “Whoever establishes a good practice in Islam will have its reward and the reward of those who act on it”, it is understood as setting a good example in doing good,

as is clear from the occasion of the hadith: the Messenger of Allah ﷺ urged charity, and a man from the Anṣār brought a large bag, and people followed him in giving charity; at that the Messenger of Allah ﷺ said what he said.

It is also understood as referring to one who brings to light and revives a Sunnah of the Messenger ﷺ, as ʿUmar (may Allah be pleased with him) did in gathering the people for the tarāwīḥ prayer in Ramaḍān, which was bringing his Sunnah ﷺ to light,
since he ﷺ led the people in the night prayer of Ramaḍān on some nights and then left it for fear that it would be made obligatory on them, as in Ṣaḥīḥ al-Bukhārī (2012).

When the Messenger of Allah ﷺ died, the fear that it would be made obligatory was gone, since legislation ceased with his death ﷺ, and the recommendation remained; so ʿUmar (may Allah be pleased with him) brought it to light. It is also part of the Sunnah of the rightly guided caliphs.

His saying (may Allah be pleased with him), “What an excellent innovation!” (in Ṣaḥīḥ al-Bukhārī, 2010), referring to bringing the tarāwīḥ prayer to light, means innovation in the linguistic sense. Similar to this is the [extra] call to prayer on Friday that ʿUthmān (may Allah be pleased with him) added,

in which the Companions (may Allah be pleased with them) agreed with him, so it is part of the Sunnah of the rightly guided caliphs. What is reported from Ibn ʿUmar (may Allah be pleased with them both), that it is an innovation, is understood—if authentic—as innovation in the linguistic sense.
It is recommended to give admonition and reminders from time to time,
because of the effect this has on hearts.
The Companions (may Allah be pleased with them) were eager for good,
as their asking him ﷺ for advice shows.
The most important thing to advise is fear of Allah, the Mighty and Majestic, which is obeying Him by carrying out His command and avoiding His prohibition.
Among the most important things to advise is hearing and obeying those in authority,
because of the worldly and otherworldly benefits this brings the Muslims.
The hadith stresses in the strongest terms the duty to hear and obey, even if the commander is a slave.
The Prophet ﷺ foretold much disagreement in his nation, and its coming about as he foretold is one of the proofs of his prophethood ﷺ.
The way of safety when disagreement arises in the religion is to hold to the Sunnah of the Prophet ﷺ and the Sunnah of the rightly guided caliphs.
The rightly guided caliphs—Abū Bakr, ʿUmar, ʿUthmān and ʿAlī (may Allah be pleased with them)—have great virtue, and they were rightly guided and guiding.
The hadith warns against everything newly invented in the religion that has no basis in it.
All innovations are misguidance; none of them is good.
The hadith combines encouragement and warning,
since in encouraging he said, “hold to”, and in warning, “beware”.
The advice to fear Allah, to hear and obey those in authority, to follow the Sunnahs and to leave innovations is of great importance,
since the Prophet ﷺ gave this advice to his Companions after they said of his admonition: “It is as though this were a farewell admonition, so advise us.”
